transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The Associated Press has called the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi
for Democratic challenger Scott Calome.
It'll become Mississippi's first black senator since Reconstruction.
It's been well over a week since Election Day.
Reporter Elise Catrine Gregg of the Gulf States Newsroom
and Mississippi Public Broadcasting says it has taken days
to tally the votes, and she attended Calome's victory party last night.
>> I was at that rally and his watch party a week ago on election night,
and if energy was high on election night,
it was through the roof yesterday.
>> We want Scott.
We want Scott.
We want Scott.
>> People I spoke with last night just seemed proud.
You know, there's a lot of joy, a lot of excitement,
and no small amount of relief.
>> Meanwhile, the other outstanding U.S. Senate race is in Alaska.
Democratic challenger Mary Piltola leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan
by a few thousand votes.
The Trump administration is calling for the controversial sale
of federal public lands to states, local governments, and tribes.
NPR's Kirk Siegler has more.
>> On page 24 of the new 28-page U.S. Department
of the Interior Strategic Plan is a brief section
that says the agency will, quote, "work to decrease the size
of the federal estate by offering to states, localities, and tribes,
the opportunity to purchase federal lands."
The plan proposes that some of the money from the sales will go back
to those entities and be put toward conserving land.
Trump's Interior Department did not immediately respond to a request
for more details, and for now it's unclear how much land would be sold.
It's also potentially legally dubious because Congress has
to approve any major federal land sale larger than 2,500 acres.
The plan drew swift criticism from Western environmentalists
who said Trump officials want to turn coveted land used by all Americans
over to industry or to states that could never afford to manage it
and would be forced to sell it.
Kirk Siegler, NPR News, Boise.
>> World leaders are meeting in Turkey
for the U.N.'s annual climate summit.
The leaders are urging each other to get tougher on global warming.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shelchi reports from Antalya, Turkey.
>> 197 nations are represented at the two-week conference,
also known as COP31, to discuss how to curb climate change.
U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres made an urgent appeal.
>> We know the truth.
Now we must act on it.
Because climate action is more than a fight over a number or a thermometer.
We are in the fight for our lives and our children's future.
>> Scientists say that global warming is set
to surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 Fahrenheit in a few years,
increasing the risk of catastrophic rising of sea level
and the collapse of ecosystems.
The U.S. administration was absent from the summit
for a second year in a row.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Antalya.
>> This is NPR.
The New York Fire Department says at least two people have died
in yesterday's building collapse in Brooklyn.
Local news reports say more bodies are being pulled from the rubble.
New York City officials say they don't know how many other people
are still missing and they don't know what caused the building to fall.
Shares in big tech company Nvidia continue to plunge again
in pre-market trading this morning.
They're down by more than 7%.
Nvidia is investigating CEO Jensen Huang, who has admitted to an affair.
News reports suggest that it was with an alleged Chinese spy.
NPR has not confirmed this reporting.
No two people have the same fingerprints.
NPR's Nate Rott reports on a new study that suggests this may also be true of monkeys.
>> The tiny ridges on the surface of your fingers and toes, hands and feet,
your fingerprints or footprints, they're called friction ridges
and they're meant to help you grip things.
Their uniqueness has also been used in forensics for humans for a long time,
as anyone who watches crime thrillers knows.
This new study published in the journal Plus One suggests these ridges could also
be used to identify individual primates too.
Scientists looked at the palm prints and footprints of 116 individual monkeys
in Brazil and found that none were the same.
More testing, they say, is also needed.
Nate Rott, NPR News.
>> On Wall Street in pre-market trading, stock futures are lower.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ is down 250 points.
This is NPR.
